coach_says: Nc6 is a normal developing move and perfectly playable against 1.h4. The slightly better plan is to grab the centre first with ...c5 or develop with ...Nf6, keeping your c-pawn free to support d5. Nothing here needs fixing.

Castling here is fine. Your knight on e5 is the target of ...Qc7 and ...Nxe5, so trading it with Nxc6 first is a touch cleaner, but getting the king safe is a sound choice and the position stays level.

Recapturing with the knight is fine, but bxc3 was a bit stronger because the pawn lands on c3 attacking the bishop on b4, so you win a tempo. It also keeps your e2 knight free to jump to g3 and chase the bishop on f5. When you have two ways to recapture, check which one also hits something.
1...c6, the Caro-Kann, is a completely sound reply to 1.e4. You plan ...d5 next to challenge White's centre. No lesson here.

bxc5 is a reasonable move and keeps the balance. The engine slightly prefers f4, hitting the e5 pawn and opening the f-file to challenge Black's strong knight on d4, but the difference is small. Do keep an eye on ...c4 hitting your queen, since ...Nxc2 can then fork queen and rook.
Rae1+ is an excellent move: Black's king is stuck in the centre and you bring a rook to the open e-file with check. Bg6+ and Qxc7 were just as good. Keep bringing pieces in against the king.

coach_says: Nc3 is a natural developing move and only slightly worse than the alternatives. It does allow ...Bb4 pinning the knight and ...d4, so Bg5 or Ne2 were a little more accurate, but your real problem is the early Qf3, which has given Black easy development. Nothing major to fix on this move.

Kd2 is fine and the endgame stays drawn. Your king heads towards Black's queenside pawns while your h-pawn ties down Black's king, which is the right plan. The other moves the engine suggests lead to the same result.
h4 is the best move here. Your king is safe on c2, so throwing your kingside pawns at Black's castled king with h4 and g5 is exactly the right plan. Keep going.
also: pawn storm against the castled king

coach_says: Be7 is about as good as anything here. Your position is already difficult because exd5 is coming and your d5 and c4 pawns are weak, so no move solves that. Developing and castling quickly is the right practical choice.

c3, preparing d4, is a normal plan. Its small drawback is that ...d5 hits e4 and your bishop on c4 at once, so you lose a little time. Nc3 or castling first keeps things simpler, but the difference is small.
Bg5 is a playable opening, the Levitsky. Black can hit back with ...c5 and ...Qb6 at your b2 pawn, so know those ideas, but the position is fine. Nf3 or c4 are the more common choices.
The position is lost whatever you play: Black has a rook for two pawns. Qd5+ is a reasonable try for checks, and keeping your queen active to look for perpetual check is the right practical approach.

When your knight is attacked by e5, put it in the centre: Nd5 is a perfect square because White has no c- or e-pawn that can ever kick it. Ng4 threatens nothing (e5 is defended by d4, f2 by queen and king), and after h3 it has to go to h6 on the edge, while d5 then gains more time by hitting your c6 knight. Ask where the knight is safe and useful, not just where it can go.

Your king is on d8 and White's rook is on d1, so ...d6 opens the d-file towards your own king. After Nb6 Rb8 exd6, the pawn on d6 can't be taken because Bxd6 loses the bishop to Rxd6+, and it cramps your whole position. Before you open a file, check whose rook and king are on it; ...b5 and ...Bb7 develop without that.
concept: opened a file to your own king
also: knight on b6 ties up rook and bishop
